 Insight From ‘Jailer 2’ to ‘Dorothy’: How The Tamil Film Box Office Has Found Its Second Wind This Year 
 As audiences embrace powerful smaller titles like ‘Dorothy’ and ‘Modha Rathiri’ along with the commercial juggernaut ‘Jailer 2’, is the Tamil box office challenging conventional ideas of sustained theatrical success? 'Jailer 2' and 'Dorothy' Sruthi Ganapathy Raman Updated on :  29 Oct 2026, 9:56 am 
 Copied 
 It’s only October, and the year is already holding signs of a record-breaking milestone for Tamil cinema. Nelson and Rajinikanth’s Jailer 2 has officially become the highest-grossing Tamil film of all time and is well on its way to becoming the first ₹1000 crore Tamil film. 
 “ Jailer 2 is inching close to ₹1000 crore. I hope this is the first Tamil film to reach there,” ruminates popular Tamil film distributor Tiruppur Subramaniam — the film has grossed ₹755.50 crore worldwide at the time of writing this article. But there is more to this than box-office numbers alone. That 2026 made room for Jailer 2 alongside the delicate, deeply powerful Dorothy is noteworthy in itself.
 You May Also Like Exclusive | Keerthy Suresh on 'Dorothy' Success, Long Theatrical Run: ‘I Was Told The Film Will Not Be A Box-Office Hit’ Tamil film industry tracker Sreedhar Pillai goes on record to say that Dorothy was profitable just on theatrical release alone. 
 “It had such a tough release window, and there was so much competition all around. But the way it became a wildfire in theatres was phenomenal,” he says. The film went against mainstream conventions and still went on to become a hit, something that was unimaginable a few years ago. 
 “The audiences have paved the way for all this. I cannot imagine Dorothy running with this kind of success even one or two years back. Earlier, these kinds of films used to run in high-end multiplexes, but today, it has gone down to the tier 2 and 3 cities and is doing really well."
 A still from 'Jailer 2' The Karthik Subbaraj film, co-starring Rishikanth , Sananth and Keerthy Suresh, tackles, with audacity, themes of masculinity and the incredible story of a trans woman’s transition. The film, made on a tight budget, has gone on to make ₹15.88 crore in India net collections, continuing to run in theatres despite its recent landing on Netflix. Reaping similar rewards is Raja Karuppasamy’s Modha Rathiri , which also co-starred Rishikanth.
 You May Also Like ‘Dorothy’ DOP Tirru on Finding Emotion in Lonely Landscapes and Filming the Climax: 'Ilaiyaraaja Sir Took It to a Divine Space' The film, which was struggling to fill in theatres during the first few days of release — it was out on August 21 — sustained terrific word of mouth. “For the first three days, there weren't people in the theatres,” points out filmmaker Karuppasamy. “But once we started giving interviews and going to the theatres, people started coming to the theatres. My film didn't have known faces, but the word of mouth was strong. For example, a person who had watched the film one day actually brought in his friends the next day, which I personally saw. This is how the film ran for 55 days.” 
 The film, through amiable performances by Anishma Anilkumar and Rishikanth, told the tragicomic story of a distraught couple forced to marry. 
 Nobody wanted to distribute Modha Rathiri, but it struck a chord with the audiences, Pillai notes. “The theatrical release is most essential. If Modha Rathiri had been released exclusively on streaming, it would've never had this kind of rave response.” Karuppasamy, who set out to explore patriarchy in modern marriages, chose comedy as a way to drive home his message.
 Raja Karuppasamy and Anishma Anilkumar in 'Modha Rathiri' You May Also Like Exclusive | Rishikanth on 'Dorothy' and Filming Climax with Sananth: 'We Didn't Realise The Magnitude Of That Kiss' “I was part of the league of debut filmmakers who wanted to really break out with their film. I was pleasantly surprised by the recognition of the film following its release on streaming,” says Karuppasamy. But the joy comes with a twinge of sadness. 
 “I am happy about the admiration, but maybe it didn't get the same level of recognition in the theatres. Not just my films, but films like Baththa and Dorothy need to make ₹50-100 crores. It's not just about money, but good films need to make commercial sense.”
 The year also produced hits which had significant star power, including Suriya’s Karuppu and Soori’s Mandaadi . But the last few months have been marked by smaller films, including Arjun-Preity Mukhundhan’s Blast and Vijay Sethupathi’s Baththa, titles that have managed to break through the noise. A lot of it also has to do with the way protagonists are written, Pillai weighs in.
 You May Also Like Balaji Tharaneetharan Talks 'Baththa', Masculinity, and Muse Vijay Sethupathi: 'He's Like Tom Hanks, Not Tom Cruise' “The template for hardcore commercial cinema has changed, and even Rajinikanth has adapted to it. Rather than insist on the usual introductory songs and four fights, the actor has allowed other characters to take on these moments, signalling a shift in how star vehicles are conceived and presented,” he says. 
 Several star-driven vehicles have failed earlier, as the tracker points out, but Jailer 2 sailed through. “With Suraj Venjaramoodu, SJ Suryah and Namo Narayana playing their parts, it delivered commercial entertainment at its best.” The blockbuster sequel’s biggest talking point turned out to be Namo Narayana’s Moorthy, a lovable goof, who goes head to head with Rajinikanth’s Muthuvel Pandian.
 It might not be an overstatement to say 2026 marks a significant shift in Tamil viewing habits as well.
 Sananth and Rishikanth in 'Dorothy' "This was once a trend largely associated with Malayalam cinema, but it has now seeped into Tamil cinema as well. Ultimately, audiences are willing to watch films of any scale, as long as they are good,” says Subramanian. With box office numbers, it’s often pertinent to keep in mind the basis of profitability, the distributor reminds. “A film is a hit only if it makes around 2-3 times the cost of its production. It's not hitting about ₹200 to ₹300 crore."
 Karuppasamy, who credits the team's incessant promotions for its streaming success, hopes to proudly parade a 100-day sticker for his film one day. “I am still promoting the film. I reached out to Aamir Khan sir to see if he would watch it, and Aju Varghese sir has also said he will watch and promote it. I want the film to reach many more audiences. I have always wanted to put up a 100-day poster for one of my films. Hopefully, that dream comes true with my next film."
